structures.name: aorta
structures.definition: The body’s main artery, rising from the heart, arching over it and running down in front of the spine.
structures.function: Carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to every artery of the body except those of the lungs.
structures.why: Its elastic wall absorbs each heartbeat and recoils, turning pulsed output into steadier flow.

notes.medicine: Ends at L4 by dividing into the common iliac arteries; an abdominal aneurysm presents as a pulsatile mass.
notes.nursing: A sudden tearing chest or back pain with unequal arm blood pressures suggests aortic dissection: escalate immediately.

structures.name: common carotid artery
structures.definition: Large artery running up each side of the neck beside the windpipe.
structures.function: Carries blood to the head and neck, dividing at the level of the upper thyroid cartilage.
structures.why: Its pulse is strong and close to the surface, so it is reliable even when blood pressure is low.

notes.nursing: Check the carotid pulse for up to 10 seconds in an unresponsive adult; never press both sides at once.
notes.medicine: Its bifurcation holds the carotid sinus (blood pressure sensor) and carotid body (oxygen sensor).

structures.name: internal carotid artery
structures.definition: Branch rising from the neck through the skull base without giving branches in the neck.
structures.function: Supplies most of the front and middle of the brain and the eye.
structures.why: A protected route through the skull base carries the bulk of the brain’s blood supply.

notes.medicine: Stenosis at its origin is a major cause of stroke and transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax).

structures.name: vertebral artery
structures.definition: Artery rising through the openings in the transverse processes of the upper six cervical vertebrae.
structures.function: Joins its partner inside the skull to supply the brainstem, cerebellum and back of the brain.
structures.why: Travelling inside the vertebrae protects it as the neck moves.

notes.physio: Screen for vertebrobasilar insufficiency (dizziness, diplopia, drop attacks) before neck manipulation.

structures.name: basilar artery
structures.definition: Single artery lying on the front of the pons, formed where the two vertebral arteries join.
structures.function: Supplies the brainstem and cerebellum and divides into the posterior cerebral arteries.
structures.why: Joining two arteries into one gives the brainstem a backup if one side is narrowed.

notes.medicine: Its occlusion causes “locked-in syndrome” and is often fatal without urgent treatment.

structures.name: subclavian artery
structures.definition: Artery arching over the first rib behind the clavicle toward the armpit.
structures.function: Supplies the arm and gives branches to the brain, chest wall and neck.
structures.why: It carries blood to the upper limb while the clavicle shields it.

notes.medicine: Becomes the axillary artery at the outer border of the first rib; compressed in thoracic outlet syndrome.

structures.name: axillary artery
structures.definition: Artery passing through the armpit from the first rib to the lower border of the teres major.
structures.function: Supplies the shoulder region and continues into the arm.
structures.why: It runs deep in the armpit, surrounded by the brachial plexus, protected by fat and muscle.

notes.medicine: Shoulder dislocations and fractures of the humeral neck can injure it.

structures.name: brachial artery
structures.definition: Main artery of the upper arm, running down its inner side to the front of the elbow.
structures.function: Supplies the arm and divides into the radial and ulnar arteries below the elbow.
structures.why: Its course in the groove beside the large flexor muscle keeps it sheltered.

notes.nursing: Blood pressure cuffs compress it; listen over it, just medial to the tendon in the elbow crease.
notes.medicine: Supracondylar fractures in children can injure it: check the radial pulse and hand perfusion.

structures.name: radial artery
structures.definition: Forearm artery running down the thumb side to the wrist.
structures.function: Supplies the forearm and hand and forms the deep palmar arch.
structures.why: Running superficially over the end of the radius makes it easy to feel and reach.

notes.nursing: The usual site for the pulse and for arterial blood gas sampling; do Allen’s test first.
notes.medicine: Common access route for coronary angiography and arterial lines.

structures.name: ulnar artery
structures.definition: Forearm artery running down the little-finger side to the wrist.
structures.function: Supplies the forearm and hand and forms the superficial palmar arch.
structures.why: With its partner on the other side, it gives the hand a double blood supply.

notes.nursing: Allen’s test checks that it can perfuse the hand before radial artery sampling.

structures.name: coeliac trunk
structures.definition: Short thick artery leaving the front of the abdominal aorta just below the diaphragm.
structures.function: Divides into the left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries.
structures.why: It supplies the foregut: oesophagus end, stomach, liver, pancreas, spleen and upper duodenum.

notes.medicine: Arises at T12; its three branches form a “tripod”.

structures.name: superior mesenteric artery
structures.definition: Artery leaving the front of the aorta just below the trunk to the upper abdominal organs.
structures.function: Supplies the small intestine, caecum, ascending colon and most of the transverse colon.
structures.why: One large vessel feeds the whole midgut through arcades in the mesentery.

notes.medicine: Its sudden occlusion causes acute mesenteric ischaemia: pain out of proportion to the examination.

structures.name: inferior mesenteric artery
structures.definition: Smaller artery leaving the front of the aorta at L3.
structures.function: Supplies the distal transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon and upper rectum.
structures.why: It feeds the hindgut, whose blood supply links with the midgut’s along the marginal artery.

notes.medicine: The splenic flexure is a watershed area prone to ischaemic colitis.

structures.name: renal artery
structures.definition: Artery leaving each side of the aorta at about L1 to enter the kidney.
structures.function: Carries about a fifth of the heart’s output to the kidney for filtering.
structures.why: The kidneys need far more blood than their size suggests, because they clean the whole circulation.

notes.medicine: Renal artery stenosis causes resistant hypertension; the right artery passes behind the inferior vena cava.

structures.name: common iliac artery
structures.definition: One of the two terminal branches of the aorta, running down and outward at the pelvic brim.
structures.function: Divides into the internal iliac artery for the pelvis and the external iliac artery for the leg.
structures.why: Splitting the aorta gives each leg and each side of the pelvis its own supply.

notes.medicine: Aortic aneurysms often extend into it.

structures.name: external iliac artery
structures.definition: Artery running along the pelvic brim to pass under the inguinal ligament.
structures.function: Carries blood to the leg; it becomes the femoral artery at the inguinal ligament.
structures.why: It is the leg’s main supply line through the pelvis.

notes.medicine: Kidney transplants are usually connected to it.

structures.name: femoral artery
structures.definition: Main artery of the thigh, starting at the groin and running down its front and inner side.
structures.function: Supplies the thigh and continues behind the knee to supply the leg.
structures.why: It is the leg’s main artery, superficial in the groin and then protected in a muscular canal.

notes.nursing: The femoral pulse is felt at the mid-inguinal point; check the groin site for bleeding after angiography.
notes.medicine: Common access for angiography and arterial lines.

structures.name: popliteal artery
structures.definition: Continuation of the femoral artery, lying deep in the hollow at the back of the knee.
structures.function: Supplies the knee and divides into the arteries of the leg.
structures.why: It is the deepest structure in the back of the knee, cushioned by fat.

notes.nursing: Its pulse is felt deep in the back of the knee with the knee slightly bent.
notes.sports: Knee dislocations can tear it; always check the foot pulses after a dislocation.

structures.name: anterior tibial artery
structures.definition: Leg artery running down the front of the interosseous membrane to the ankle.
structures.function: Supplies the front of the leg and continues onto the foot.
structures.why: It feeds the muscles that lift the foot.

notes.sports: Swelling in the front compartment can compress it (compartment syndrome).

structures.name: posterior tibial artery
structures.definition: Leg artery running down the back of the calf and behind the medial malleolus into the sole.
structures.function: Supplies the back of the leg and the sole of the foot.
structures.why: It carries blood to the weight-bearing sole.

notes.nursing: Its pulse is felt behind the medial malleolus; check it in peripheral vascular assessments.

structures.name: dorsalis pedis artery
structures.definition: Artery on the top of the foot, continuing from the leg artery that runs down the front of the shin.
structures.function: Supplies the top of the foot and links with the arteries of the sole.
structures.why: It completes a loop of blood supply around the foot.

notes.nursing: Its pulse is felt on the top of the foot, lateral to the big-toe extensor tendon; absent in a minority of people.

structures.name: superior vena cava
structures.definition: Large vein entering the top of the right atrium.
structures.function: Returns blood from the head, neck, arms and upper chest.
structures.why: One short, wide vein lets the whole upper body drain into the heart with little resistance.

notes.nursing: Central venous catheter tips should sit in its lower part, just above the right atrium.

structures.name: inferior vena cava
structures.definition: The largest vein, running up the right side of the spine to the heart.
structures.function: Returns blood from the legs, pelvis and abdomen.
structures.why: It carries the largest volume of returning blood, so it is the widest vein.

notes.nursing: In late pregnancy, lying flat compresses it; tilt the patient to the left.

structures.name: internal jugular vein
structures.definition: Large vein running down the side of the neck beside the carotid artery.
structures.function: Drains blood from the brain, face and neck.
structures.why: It carries the brain’s venous blood straight down to the heart.

notes.nursing: Jugular venous pressure is assessed with the patient at 45°; it reflects right atrial pressure.
notes.medicine: The right one is the preferred route for ultrasound-guided central venous catheters.

structures.name: subclavian vein
structures.definition: Vein passing under the clavicle, in front of its artery, from the armpit to the base of the neck.
structures.function: Drains the arm and joins the internal jugular vein.
structures.why: A wide, fixed vein that stays open even when blood volume is low.

notes.nursing: Central lines inserted here carry a risk of pneumothorax; check the chest X-ray afterwards.

structures.name: cephalic vein
structures.definition: Superficial vein running up the thumb side of the forearm and arm into the groove between the chest and shoulder muscles.
structures.function: Drains the outer side of the hand and arm into the axillary vein.
structures.why: Running just under the skin, it carries blood up the arm without being compressed by muscle.

notes.nursing: At the wrist it is the “intern’s vein”: large and straight, good for cannulation.

structures.name: basilic vein
structures.definition: Superficial vein running up the little-finger side of the forearm and inner arm before diving deep.
structures.function: Drains the inner side of the hand and arm into the axillary vein.
structures.why: It joins the deep veins halfway up the arm, giving a route for central catheters.

notes.nursing: A common route for PICC lines; it lies close to the brachial artery and median nerve at the elbow.

structures.name: median cubital vein
structures.definition: Short superficial vein crossing the front of the elbow between the two main arm veins.
structures.function: Links the two superficial veins of the arm.
structures.why: It is large, superficial and anchored by the bicipital aponeurosis, so it rolls little.

notes.nursing: The first choice for venepuncture: superficial, well anchored and away from nerves.

structures.name: hepatic portal vein
structures.definition: Vein formed behind the pancreas by the union of the splenic and superior mesenteric veins.
structures.function: Carries nutrient-rich blood from the gut, spleen and pancreas to the liver.
structures.why: Routing absorbed food and toxins through the liver first lets it process them before they reach the body.

notes.medicine: Portal hypertension (usually cirrhosis) opens collaterals: oesophageal varices, caput medusae, haemorrhoids.

structures.name: femoral vein
structures.definition: Deep vein of the thigh, lying beside its artery in the groin.
structures.function: Drains the leg toward the external iliac vein.
structures.why: It carries most of the leg’s blood back from the deep muscles.

notes.nursing: A common site of deep vein thrombosis; it lies medial to the femoral artery (remember NAVY).

structures.name: great saphenous vein
structures.definition: The longest vein in the body, running up the inner side of the leg from the foot to the groin.
structures.function: Drains the superficial tissues of the leg into the deep vein in the groin.
structures.why: A superficial channel lets skin and fat drain while deep veins carry the muscle blood.

notes.nursing: Lies just in front of the medial malleolus: a reliable site for a cut-down in an emergency.
notes.medicine: Harvested for coronary artery bypass grafts; varicose veins often start at its valves.

structures.name: small saphenous vein
structures.definition: Superficial vein running up the back of the calf from behind the lateral malleolus.
structures.function: Drains the outer foot and back of the leg into the deep vein behind the knee.
structures.why: It drains the calf skin into the deep system.

notes.medicine: Its valves can fail, causing varicose veins at the back of the calf.
